children.author: ButlerianJihad
solyin
children.text: On the other hand, Bank of America just deployed Copilot to all of their employees.

We've heard of "Shadow IT" now we have "Shadow SWE" and "Shadow CI/CD".

It used to be that someone wanted unfettered Internet access, and they were disgruntled with the company's firewall or proxy policy, and so they brought in a modem, and hooked it up to their desktop PC, and started dialing out on some analog line that the company didn't even know they had. Then it's all fine for 3 years until some malware gets discovered, and then IT discovers who-all had unauthorized lines that weren't being scanned or filtered at the company firewall. Same thing happens with WiFi APs today, of course.

I was working for a company that really offered no in-house software or tools to run. But my new supervisor was asking me to closely track my time. So I signed up for some SaaS that would let me log activities and track my timeslices, so I could show a graph or table later on and see what I was doing. I used it for a few weeks. It was real effective. But what I realized down the line, was that all the notes I was typing into this 3rd-party SaaS, were revealing company confidential information. And ultimately, I felt very uncomfortable about revealing what I was doing, on an unannounced and private project, and without authorization or even notifying my employer's IT department. So I shut it all down, and I had to do it with pen and paper, but that felt secure enough.

So if people are going to feel empowered by vibe coding their own bespoke apps, I hope their IT department comes down like a ton of bricks, and tells them to knock it off. Because it is not worth the tech debt, support costs, and ultimately the massive security problems and infoleaks. If your employer won't give you what you need in these terms, then maybe it's just not important to them in the first place.

children.author: chasd00
kiwicopple
children.text: hey - supabase ceo/cofounder here. Please tell your little sister that I’m happy supabase could be a small part of her builder journey, and good luck with her app. My email is in my bio if she has any product feedback

I’ve had two separate similar experiences. The most impressive was my little sister publishing an app on both Google and Apple AppStore’s with subscription payment support. She didn’t even know what an Apple developer account was. I gave her a three line prompt to get started and then she took it from there. She built an LMS for HS students that gets them in shape for college admissions. She has a supabase backend, AI generated videos, quizzes, more content, and all the usual mobile app bells and whistles, she made it through all the paperwork of App Store submission/review/publishing on both platforms including inviting some beta testers. Her workflow was telling ChatGPT what she wanted and then asking that model to talk to claudecode. It doesn’t sound like much but keep in mind she has absolutely zero code or tech experience. I told her she did about a $75k project on her own in maybe 1/5 the time and it blew her away.

It may be a success or maybe not who knows but she did it. I think she has 4 or 5 paying customers.

source.text:
My SO works in legal and regulatory compliance, she needed a small app (worflow with a form and a validation process), CTO said they could not do it, too complicated, would cost 15 days for a freelance and rejected it. She called it BS, and the next day she spent the morning with ChatGPT using their internal Microsoft-based tooling, and the app was done. She was hyped for the day, with a feeling of accomplishment and is already thinking of another project. And I'm hearing similar stories every week.

So yes, LLM have positive impacts in many business domains, but seeing people happy and enpowered with their home-made little apps, I think it's the best.
